Inanda Land Grab revisited

By: Mart-Marie Faure | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We revisit the Tea Estate near Durban where a fierce battle has been raging for almost ten years about ownership of farmland.

Unique Selling Point:
We revisit Tea estate Inanda near Durban where illegal farm invasions and illegal sale of farmland has been ongoing since 2016 . Landgrabs have escalated and racial tension is building daily.

Summary:
In 2018 we covered a story about land invasion in Tea Estate Inanda north of Durban.
The Chief in the area claims the land belongs to the Qadi clan and he has the right over the land.
Since our story aired the land invasions continued and the farmers obtained a court order against ha AmaQadi clan to stop them from selling and allocating land the farmers say belong to them. Large homes – including a three star hotel- have been built on the land. Roads, water and electricity have been provided to some of the dwellings by the municipality. The farmers association questioned why amenities are provided to unregistered properties but have not had any response. . In 2019 the High Courts ruled in favour of the farmers , ordering a halt to the sale or allocation of land by the chief, Inkose Mqoqi Ngcono. The farmersI provided title deeds , proving that the land belongs to them. They farmed mostly sugar cane. The order included the demolition of structures. No structures have been demolished to date. Farmers fear that there will be unrest if they take action.

The disputed land comprises farms that have been carved up, sold, cleared and built on.
. The farmers sought a final interdict to prevent Chief Ngcobo or his Nduna from inciting people to “invade, carve, fence, erect structures” such as houses on the land. In court papers, they contend that people occupying the land had said they paid between R20,000 and R50,000 to Nduna of Ngcobo.
Ngcobo claims the disputed land, along with land in Ndwedwe, Ballito and Umhlanga, has been part of the AmaQadi clan land for centuries. He disputes the Tea Estate farmers’ contention that their title deeds are proof that their families bought the land more than 100 years ago. The farmers say they have been paying rates and fees for other municipal services.
When we were there just more than 4 farms were impacted , seven years later 700 hectares have been invaded and luxury houses built. Protesting farmers have been intimidated with one farmer kidnapped, seriously beaten and his house petrol bombed( Video available) Other farmers had their tractors and sheds burnt to the ground and their lives threatened. Our source said that this will be his last year of farming as he won’t have enough land left and will have to let go of his 250 workers. Not any of the farmers have been compensated for their land.
The farmer’s attorney has approached the provincial police and government departments without any success.
There have been numerous consultations and meetings with police including Mkwanazi and Masemola but the 160 dockets have not been investigated. Verulam And Inanda police have not offered any assistance.
